nameStory: The name "tall hairy agrimony" tells you exactly what you're looking at - this is the tallest of our local agrimonies and quite fuzzy to the touch! The word "agrimony" comes from the ancient Greek "argemone," meaning "healing to the eyes," reflecting this plant's long history as a medicinal herb. Indigenous peoples have used it for generations to treat ailments like diarrhea and fever.
description: Tall hairy agrimony is a shoulder-high perennial wildflower that's a surprising member of the rose family, though it looks nothing like a typical rose. This fuzzy-stemmed plant grows 2-5 feet tall with compound leaves that have an odd number of leaflets arranged feather-like along the stem. In mid to late summer, it produces slender spikes of tiny yellow flowers that later develop into distinctive hooked seed pods that will grab onto your socks and pet fur. Despite its delicate appearance, it's a sturdy plant that comes back year after year from the same root system.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 5-9 toothed leaflets arranged like a feather, with tiny leaflets scattered between the larger ones. The leaves feel soft and fuzzy, almost velvety, and have a fresh, slightly bitter smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers, each about the size of a pencil eraser, arranged in long slender spikes at the top of the plant. Each flower has 5 petals and blooms from bottom to top along the spike.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small grooved seed pods covered in hooked bristles that feel like tiny velcro when touched. These "hitchhiker" seeds will eagerly attach to clothing, fur, and feathers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 2-5 feet tall in an upright, somewhat branching pattern. The entire plant feels soft and hairy to the touch, especially the stems which are noticeably fuzzy.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctly hairy stems that feel soft and fuzzy when you run your fingers along them. The hairs are dense enough to give the whole stem a grayish-green, almost woolly appearance.

habitat: Look for tall hairy agrimony along woodland edges, in open woods, and beside trails where it gets partial sun but some shade. It prefers moist, rich soils and often grows alongside other woodland edge plants like goldenrod and asters. You'll commonly find it in that transitional zone between deep forest and open meadow.

seasonality.spring: New fuzzy leaves emerge in late spring, growing into their characteristic compound shape. The soft, hairy stems begin their upward growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from July through August, with bright yellow flower spikes most noticeable in mid to late summer. This is the best time for identification when flowers and leaves are both present.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the infamous hooked seed pods mature, becoming the plant's most noticeable feature as they cling to anything that brushes past. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and scattered seed pods that may persist into early winter before breaking down completely.

funFact: Tall hairy agrimony's seeds are nature's original velcro - their hooked bristles inspired part of the design for modern hook-and-loop fasteners, and a single plant can produce hundreds of these clingy hitchhikers that can travel for miles on a single animal!
confusionNotes: The compound leaves might make you think of wild roses or brambles, but agrimony's leaves are much softer and fuzzier, and it has those distinctive yellow flower spikes instead of typical rose-like blooms. Remember: roses have thorns and agrimony has fuzz!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the rose family, agrimony looks nothing like what most people expect from a "rose" - no thorns, no showy flowers, and a completely different growth habit. This shows how diverse plant families can be, united more by flower structure and genetics than obvious appearance.
compareHints: Tall hairy agrimony lives up to its name by being the tallest and fuzziest of New England's agrimonies. Roadside agrimony is shorter with less hair, while swamp agrimony prefers wetter spots and has smaller flowers. The dense, soft hairiness covering the whole plant is your best clue that you've found the "tall hairy" species rather than its smoother relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Roadside agrimony differs from tall hairy agrimony by preferring sunnier, more disturbed sites rather than woodland edges.
Swamp agrimony differs from tall hairy agrimony and roadside agrimony primarily by habitat - it's the wetland specialist of the group.
Among New England's agrimonies, downy agrimony is distinguished by its exceptionally soft, velvety stem hairs and preference for drier sites.
